“Better to be a country of sheep led by a lion than a country of lions led by a sheep.” ---Attributed to Chabrias, a Greek military commander, circa 357 BC  President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s decision to leave the response to China’s latest provocations in the hands of Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro raises yet again serious questions about his willingness to confront a challenge that demands presidential leadership. Lazaro is the same official who caused the Philippine delegation’s walkout during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech at the United Nations. Whatever one’s view of that incident, the larger question remains: when the Philippines is being insulted and challenged on the international stage, where is the President’s voice?  Leadership means stepping up when the country needs you most. It means taking responsibility, standing firm in the face of pressure, and making it clear that the Philippines will not be intimidated by a foreign power. A president cannot simply delegate the hard decisions and expect his subordinates to carry the political burden. There are moments when the nation needs to see its commander-in-chief take charge and demonstrate the resolve expected of the office.  The concerns surrounding Vice President Sara Duterte and her political alignment are already serious enough, with questions about possible Chinese influence deserving proper scrutiny and evidence. The last thing the country needs is a president whose response to Beijing’s provocations leaves Filipinos wondering whether their government has the determination to defend national sovereignty. We have seen what many regarded as a weak response to an earlier insulting statement from the Chinese Embassy. Are we now going to witness another?  For crying out loud, Mr. President, how many times must China test the limits before you draw a clear line? Diplomacy has its place, but diplomacy without resolve risks being mistaken for weakness. The Filipino people deserve to know that their President will stand up for their country when it matters most.  Mr. President, the question is no longer whether the Philippines should stand its ground. It is whether you are prepared to lead the country in doing so. When is enough finally enough? @bongbongmarcos @risahontiveros @senatePH @HouseofRepsPH @DFAPHL @GiboTeodoroJr

TLDR: Ukraine, Nato  training, lativa to ukraine merc line, Oper APOLLOSHOOTER  COMMANDER’S BRIEFING  Subject: CFB Wainwright Training Area Incident – 17 October 2026  As of: 19 October 2026 (morning)  Classification: Unclassified / Open-source summary Bottom Line Up Front A grass fire during a live-fire training exercise at CFB Wainwright, Alberta, overran soldiers of C Company, 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. Four soldiers are dead and 39 are wounded (19 critically). The fire was known for hours and judged non-threatening until an uncommon wind shift drove it roughly one kilometre in 30–60 seconds. Officials have ruled out terrorism and oil/gas infrastructure involvement. Exact ignition source remains under investigation. No public evidence of outside interference. Situation  Location: CFB Wainwright training ranges, Alberta (~200 km southeast of Edmonton). Unit: C Company, 3 PPCLI (Edmonton-based), approximately 84 soldiers on the affected ranges. Part of a larger ~350-person battalion element. Mission: Exercise APOLLO SHOOTER – high-intensity combat training with live munitions. Preparing for NATO deployment to Latvia (spring) and Global Response Task Force standby. Activities included hand-grenade practice and a section-level attack on a simulated enemy. Conditions: Fire index assessed as low. Environment Canada recorded strong wind gusts (reported up to ~80–100 km/h range). Forecasts had warned of high winds.  Timeline (approximate, local time)  Hours prior to ~1600: Range control aware of a grass fire ~1 km away; assessed as controlled. ~1600, 17 Oct: Wind shifts; fire advances rapidly and overtakes the administrative area of the section-attack range. Soldiers report going from no visible fire to fire on top of them in under a minute. Evening 17 Oct: Fire spreads beyond base fence into municipal district. Multi-agency response (ground and air assets). Contained overnight. No civilian evacuations. 18 Oct: Casualties confirmed, next-of-kin notified, public briefing by Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland (1st Canadian Division) and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. PM Mark Carney statements. Flags at half-mast.  Casualties (confirmed)  Killed (4): Sgt. Morgan Wong (Edmonton; Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with 3 PPCLI) Pte. Shaun Farrell (Prince Albert, SK) Pte. Aidan Goulding (North Vancouver, BC) Pte. Hayden Lykkemark (Langley, BC)  Wounded (39): 19 critical (many severe burns), remainder stable or ambulatory. Treated across Edmonton, Calgary, Red Deer, and other facilities. Early unconfirmed reports cited up to seven fatalities; official number is four.  Cause Assessment  Official position: Grass fire in the training area, driven by uncommonly strong and rapid wind shift. Fire originated within the training area and crossed established fire guards. Preliminary military sources (Global News) indicate a munition from the live exercise likely ignited the grass. Multiple ordnance types were in use (grenades, grenade launchers, small arms). Ruled out by officials: Oil/gas infrastructure involvement (base has numerous wells; initial checks showed no damage), outside interference, and terrorist activity (DND statement: “no indications”). Internal military reports obtained by media described a “smoldering” fire becoming a “wall of flame.” Exact ignition point and whether any munition or secondary event contributed remain under investigation.  Current Status and Response Fire is held/contained. No ongoing threat to civilians. Mass casualty response included significant ground ambulances, air assets, and Code Orange activation at hospitals. Canadian Blood Services has issued calls for donors. Unit and families are receiving support. Investigation  Fire marshal on site for cause. Canadian Forces National Investigation Service (military police) and RCMP involved. Board of Inquiry expected (standard after CAF death; can compel evidence and produce recommendations). Timeline estimated at weeks to months given complexity and casualty numbers. Findings on public release not yet confirmed.  Intelligence, Rumors, and Assessment Confirmed / high-confidence elements  Training accident amplified by weather. No public indicators of deliberate attack or sabotage. DND and commander statements are consistent on this point. Communications lockdown on base after the incident is normal protocol.  Circulating claims and OSINT notes (assessed as low-to-moderate reliability or already contradicted)  Early reports of a live round striking a gas well/line and causing a major explosion (Global News sources; later rejected by Maj.-Gen. Rutland and DND). NASA FIRMS satellite detections of heat on the range hours earlier (reported ~12:17 and ~14:49 local). Consistent with a known/monitored smoldering fire; does not prove a different cause. OSINT outlets (e.g., Prime Rogue) highlight the timing gap between detections and DND’s “approximately 4 p.m. ignited” language. Social media speculation comparing wind speed to other fires, unconfirmed seismic events, or alleging cover-up. Limited traction; no evidence of coordinated information operation. Some international statements (e.g., Zelenskyy) referred to “explosion and fire”; official Canadian accounts emphasize the grass fire and wind.  Intelligence judgment  No reporting from CSIS or foreign intelligence services treating this as a security incident. Current evidence supports an internal training/range-safety event. Primary open questions for investigators: exact ignition source, range-control decision to continue training, fire-behavior factors (topography, vegetation, wind), and whether safety protocols require revision. Implications and Recommendations for Command  Readiness impact: C Company of 3 PPCLI is degraded; Latvia deployment timeline may require assessment. Range safety review likely across CAF live-fire areas, especially under elevated wind forecasts. Public and family communications will remain sensitive until Board of Inquiry progresses. Monitor for further medical updates on the 19 critical cases and any secondary investigations.  Open questions: Specific munition or activity that ignited the fire; precise distance and path of the wind-driven front; full details of range-control decisions; final injury outcomes. Further updates expected as the formal inquiry proceeds. This briefing is based on open-source reporting and official statements as of 19 October 2026.

There are almost certainly dozens, perhaps a hundred or more individuals in the country who are at various stages of planning destructive or criminal acts.  History and current security assessments show that the decisive factor is rarely the existence of such people; it is whether one of them moves from private conviction to action and carries it through.  That step does not require a large organisation or perfect coordination. One person, sufficiently committed, is enough.  On that basis the question is less whether something serious will happen than when.  The rough arithmetic is uncomfortable but straightforward. Of the roughly four million people in the UK who belong to the communities from which most of the relevant radicalisation data are drawn, government and polling figures have repeatedly indicated that a small but non-trivial minority hold views that can reasonably be described as radical.  Even if one takes a conservative reading of those figures, say around 3 % & then assumes that only a fraction of that minority (1 percent or less) is prepared to move from belief to violence, the residual number is still measured in the thousands. Within that pool it is not unreasonable to expect a few hundred individuals who combine the necessary mindset with the opportunity or the will to act.  Most will never do so. Some will. The statistical pattern does not require every radicalised person to become an attacker; it only requires that the number who do remains low enough to be predictable rather than exceptional.  I do not fear those individuals in the way some might expect. What I fear is the response that follows if ordinary people find themselves in the middle of an incident and try to stop it.  I am a British citizen whose family connections in this country reach back roughly to the eighth century. That history does not confer special rights, but it does shape the sense of obligation one feels toward family, neighbours, and the place itself. Under present conditions I am not free to defend my family, myself, or, for example, an elderly person being attacked in the street without first calculating the likely legal consequences.  The law formally permits reasonable force in self-defence or the defence of others, yet the practical reality is that anyone who uses force must be prepared for investigation, possible arrest, and the risk that a court will later decide the force was excessive. That calculation—how many years might I serve for intervening—has become part of the decision in the moment. For many people it is enough to tip the balance toward inaction.  Radical behaviour by particular individuals is therefore not the central problem. The larger difficulty is that successive governments have treated high levels of migration, including from regions with known integration and security difficulties, as a settled policy objective rather than a contingency that must be tightly managed.  The result is a population containing both people who integrate without difficulty and a persistent minority who do not. When the consequences of that policy appear on the street, the same system that enabled the scale of arrivals has also narrowed the lawful options available to those who live with the outcomes.   Citizens are told that the state will handle the risk, yet when an incident occurs in real time the state is often not present, and the citizen who acts is then judged by standards that appear stricter than those applied to the original offender.  That asymmetry is the only thing I actually fear. The existence of dangerous individuals is an old and recurring fact of human societies. The newer and more corrosive fact is the combination of policy that increases their number with a legal and institutional environment that treats decisive intervention by ordinary people as the greater danger.

Meta censored the No Kings Instagram account during a nationwide campaign and is now backtracking on its excuses.  My investigative analysis examines the hours-long administrative lockout, the people responsible for Meta’s enforcement systems and the similarities with Meta’s treatment of political accounts during Brazil’s presidential election.  I've included 21 technical questions that Congress should put directly to Meta’s engineers and data scientists under oath, backed by the company's system logs. They can be found on my Substack which is free - link in my bio.  💡 This is an independent technical investigation, not an endorsement of No Kings or its politics. No matter who you support, Meta's ability to silence a political organisation when it needs to communicate at the most important time, should concern everyone.  Here's what happened:  On 17 October, Meta suspended the official Instagram account of the No Kings Coalition during a nationwide campaign that was aimed at encouraging Americans to vote early in the 3 November midterm elections. Almost 3,000 events were taking place across the United States. Organisers lost access to their account at approximately 1:30pm Eastern Time, when they needed it to communicate with participants.  Meta initially blamed excessive posting, sharing, and commenting. The following day, its Vice President of Communications, Andy Stone, changed the explanation. Meta now claims that software using Claude AI was reading Instagram profiles, posts and hashtags at 4 times the normal rate.  The account became publicly visible again after approximately 90 minutes, but organisers couldn’t publish anything until Meta restored access hours later at 5:33pm.  Meta censored a political organisation during a national voting campaign, blamed its own automation, then claimed its automated systems had detected another automated tool. Meta admitted the suspension was wrong, but none of its explanations account for what happened from a technical standpoint.  Meta’s response is exactly what independent technical experts like me have warned about. I point this out because we can’t allow tech companies to avoid responsibility and accountability for their actions by blaming AI.  Tech companies are blaming everything but themselves. Meta is a company whose technology can infer what flavour of ice cream a 7-year-old likes from something her uncle’s dog posted on Instagram in 2020, yet apparently can’t explain why its own systems censored a political organisation at one of the most critical moments in its history.  Meta keeps changing its explanation  On 17 October, Andy Stone wrote:  🔈 "When accounts post, share or comment at very high frequencies it can trigger automated systems. That's what happened with the No Kings IG account in the lead up to today's day of action. Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error. Everything is now working as…"  💡 Stone blamed unusually frequent activity by the account itself, but the organisers disputed this, saying they’d published only a handful of posts and were livestreaming the events. Given how easily Meta’s own records could prove or disprove that claim, I suspect the company needed a more convincing explanation.  A day later, Stone provided a different explanation, saying the activity was primarily the account’s "reading" behaviour.  🔈"We have continued to dig into the root cause here and would like to offer an update. Our engineering team discovered that the spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s “reading” behavior.  Specifically, our network security systems detected the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags, the rate of which sharply increased (~4x volume) in intense bursts on October 17.  These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems.   This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline. An automated re-review of the removal action an hour later recognized that shouldn’t have happened and restored the account. It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account.  We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error."  💡 Posting and reading are completely different activities, something a competent developer or data scientist could identify within minutes by examining the activity logs. Publishing posts, sharing content and commenting involve sending information to Instagram. Reading profiles, posts and hashtags involves requesting information from Instagram.  Meta initially blamed the organisation’s publishing activity. Its engineers then identified reading activity instead.  Stone should explain what evidence supported his first and second statement.  Meta blamed Claude without identifying who was responsible.  In his revised statement, Stone said Meta’s security systems had detected "the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags".  Meta explicitly named Anthropic’s AI software but didn’t identify the tool, who operated it or whether the No Kings organisers had authorised it.  Is Meta suggesting that using Claude to access Instagram is prohibited? If so, which policy was violated? If not, why did Meta suspend the organisation’s account instead of restricting the automated requests? Meta claims activity increased fourfold  Stone said the rate of requests "sharply increased (~4x volume) in intense bursts".  Four times what?  If an account normally receives 100 requests during a particular period, four times that means 400. If it normally receives 100,000, the increase means 400,000.  My LinkedIn posts typically reach between 2,000 and 250,000 readers, while my posts on X range from 500 to 1.2 million. Sudden increases in activity are normal on social media.  Stone’s reference to "intense bursts" sounds alarming but provides no meaningful technical information without the actual request counts, timeframe and frequency. Even a small number of automated requests can arrive in intense bursts. What Meta hasn’t established is why those requests justified suspending the organisation’s account.  Reader counts and automated requests are different measurements, so the size of an audience alone cannot establish whether Meta’s security threshold was reasonable.  Without the actual numbers, the measurement period and Meta’s security thresholds, the figure doesn’t tell us anything.  The No Kings Coalition was coordinating almost 3,000 events. Increased activity involving its Instagram account was entirely predictable.  Meta is using a percentage without providing the numbers needed to determine if the activity justified suspending a political organisation.  Meta described automated reading as a security threat  Stone said the requests "resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems".  I founded a venture-backed cybersecurity company in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built the first security chatbots in the world - they automated actions on platforms like Slack, HipChat, Messenger, and Telegram between 2015 and 2019.   I can say with confidence that automated activity isn’t inherently a security violation. No competent cybersecurity professional, test automation specialist, or chatbot developer would automatically classify automation as malicious. That makes no technical sense. Search engines, monitoring tools, research applications and AI assistants make billions of automated requests every hour of every day.   Tech companies have systems that are designed to identify excessive traffic, restrict access credentials and block requests that violate their policies.  Does Meta apply the same restrictions to people using its own AI assistant, Muse, to automate interactions with Facebook and Instagram? If not, why? Meta admitted the suspension was wrong but continued to restrict their account  Stone claimed an automated review recognised the suspension was wrong and restored the account approximately an hour later. This is disingenuous. Meta restored public visibility, but the organisers remained locked out for hours. By saying the account had been restored, Stone concealed the fact that Meta was still preventing the organisation from publishing. Even when explaining a mistake of this magnitude, Meta chose language that obscured what actually happened.  The No Kings organisers reported that their Instagram page became publicly visible again after approximately 90 minutes, but they still couldn’t use it. People managing the account remained locked out until 5:33pm Eastern Time.  Meta’s own automated review had already decided that the suspension was wrong, yet the organisers remained unable to publish posts or communicate with supporters during their nationwide campaign.  Stone later said that restoring administrative access took additional time. Why? The only credible explanation in my view, is that restoring meaningful access required a Meta employee with the necessary authority. That suggests someone had to approve the reversal of a suspension Meta had already admitted was wrong. Meta should identify who controlled that decision, who authorised the restoration and why the organisers were kept locked out.  Restoring an Instagram page that its organisers still can’t use doesn’t restore their ability to communicate. Meta’s decision to censor them continued affecting the organisation after its own systems had recognised the suspension was wrong.  Meta’s apology doesn’t explain who made the decisions  Stone described the original enforcement action as "clearly taken in error". There’s nothing clear about it. It’s clear to me that the opposite to what he says is more likely to be true.  An automated system doesn’t independently decide which behaviour violates Instagram’s policies, especially when it comes to such prominent accounts.  The No Kings Coalition is one of America’s most prominent anti-Trump movements, organising nationwide demonstrations that involve millions of people across thousands of locations. Suspending its Instagram account during a major mobilisation campaign was a politically significant decision with predictable consequences.  Given the organisation’s prominence, the timing and the public backlash, multiple Meta teams and senior managers had to be involved in decisions about the suspension and restoration. Zuckerberg himself would have been involved, given his hands-on approach to major content moderation decisions.  This wasn’t simply a software error. People made the decisions, and Meta’s automated systems executed them. Restoring public visibility while keeping organisers locked out required separate enforcement decisions that Meta has yet to explain.  Meta’s records can identify which individuals reviewed the incident, who authorised changes, whether senior executives were briefed and why restoring full access took hours.  This isn’t the first recent case involving Meta censoring political communications during an election.  I wrote article 20 hours ago to explain how in Brazil, Meta blocked the sitting president (Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva) from running normal paid Instagram promotions while its algorithms and WhatsApp recommended his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.   Its AI refused basic Lula campaign material but produced the equivalent for Bolsonaro. Some of Meta’s staff flagged the unequal treatment in real time and escalated it; the company later offered shifting technical excuses that don’t match the dates or the fact that Bolsonaro’s campaign kept using the same tools Lula couldn’t access.  During the election, Meta ran over 1,600 political ads that researchers found were illegal, almost all paid for in US dollars, and only reclassified or removed them after they’d already been shown up to 171.1 million times. Complaints about account suspensions increased 585% during the election year.  The Brazil case doesn’t establish that the No Kings suspension was coordinated or deliberate. But it does establish another example of politically consequential account restrictions that Meta attributed to technical failures.  Meta controls when political organisations and parties can publish, advertise, appear in recommendations and communicate with their audiences. For high-profile accounts, Meta’s executives are responsible for making those decisions, not automated systems. Meta must explain what its systems actually did  Meta has logs that record absolutely everything. They know precisely what triggered the suspension, who or what caused it, which restrictions were imposed and which employees were responsible for each and every action. It also knows why organisers remained locked out after the suspension was reversed.  Meta might not document every decision made by its employees, but its system logs contain the technical evidence needed to explain what happened, unless those records have been deleted.  The public deserves to know why Mark Zuckerberg’s company is censoring political organisations and individuals in ways that just happen to favour the White House’s political agenda, cutting them off from their audiences precisely when they need to communicate most.  Congress should summon the engineers and data scientists responsible for these systems, put them under oath and demand specific technical answers backed by system logs. They shouldn’t be allowed to hide behind corporate statements or blame automation for decisions made by people.  21 questions Meta should answer  Meta’s engineers and data scientists should answer these questions and provide the technical records, internal communications, and enforcement logs to support their answers. Calling policy staff is pointless. They’ll either deflect or lack the technical knowledge to explain what actually happened.  Why did Andy Stone initially blame excessive posting, sharing and commenting when Meta later blamed reading activity? What evidence supported his first statement, who approved it and when did Meta establish that the explanation was incorrect?  What constitutes fair and acceptable use of Instagram by automated tools? Which activities are permitted, what limits apply, and what specific policy did the alleged Claude tool violate?  Do the same restrictions apply to Meta’s own AI assistant, Muse? Can people use Muse to automate reading, posting and interacting with Instagram and Facebook? If so, why was No Kings suspended for alleged automation, and does Meta apply the same enforcement thresholds to its own AI tools and competing services?  What information was the tool accessing? Was it reading publicly available content, using an authenticated account or attempting to access private information?  What does the fourfold increase actually represent? How many requests occurred, over what period, and what was the normal level of activity? Is a fourfold increase an established threshold for suspending all Instagram accounts, or was a different threshold applied to No Kings? Provide the exact measurements, enforcement thresholds and comparable records showing how Meta treats other accounts experiencing the same increase.  Which security restriction triggered the suspension? Was the decision based on request frequency, suspicious authentication, account behaviour or another classification? Identify the exact policy and technical conditions that triggered enforcement.  Why did Meta suspend No Kings instead of restricting the software making the requests? What evidence established that the organisation was responsible? Why weren’t regular security controls, including IP blocking, rate limiting or access-token restrictions, sufficient?  Did Meta classify No Kings as a politically sensitive account? Were its security thresholds, monitoring arrangements or enforcement procedures different from those applied to other big or contraversial accounts? Provide its account classifications and any associated enforcement policies.  Did any Meta employee manually review, classify, restrict or change settings associated with No Kings before or during the suspension? Identify every action, its timestamp, the employee or team responsible and the reason recorded.  What happened during the automated review that reversed the suspension? Which original finding was overturned, what evidence caused the reversal and which restrictions did the review actually remove?  Why were organisers still locked out after Meta recognised that the suspension was wrong? Which separate restriction remained active, why wasn’t it automatically removed and who or what eventually removed it?  Did any Meta employee manually restore administrative access? Provide the audit records showing when access was restored, which systems were involved and whether an employee intervened.  What happened to scheduled posts, livestreams, notifications and other communications during the suspension? How many people would otherwise have received those communications, and did Meta measure the disruption?  How many political organisations have experienced comparable suspensions? How often has Meta blamed automated activity for restrictions that subsequent reviews found were incorrect? Provide figures for suspensions during elections, protests and other major political events.  Did Meta communicate with any US government official, political campaign, intelligence agency or external organisation about No Kings before or during the suspension? Identify the participants, dates, subjects discussed and whether any communication concerned account restrictions or content distribution.  Will Meta permit independent investigators to examine the account classifications, security logs, enforcement records and restoration history? If not, why?  Were any manual configuration changes, overrides, blocklists or changes to enforcement thresholds applied to No Kings or associated hashtags within 72 hours of the suspension? Identify every change, who authorised it, when it took effect and if it was reversed later on.  Did Meta open an internal security or engineering incident involving No Kings before, during or after the suspension? Provide the incident severity, timestamps, assigned teams, tickets and relevant internal communications between security, engineering, public policy and trust and safety employees.  Does Meta use automated account restrictions or reduced content distribution for accounts involved in political mobilisation? Identify the policies, account classifications, automated enforcement conditions and any testing programmes that can restrict political accounts during periods of unusually high engagement.  Can Meta establish that No Kings would have been suspended under exactly the same conditions if it had been a commercial brand, celebrity or non-political organisation? Provide comparable enforcement records and explain if the coalition’s political classification influenced the decision.  Did Meta’s systems suspend No Kings because of a standard security policy, a special account-level configuration or a manual decision implemented through automation? Provide the configuration history, original enforcement trigger, account-specific settings and audit records needed to establish which explanation is correct.  Meta should not be allowed to answer these questions with another statement about automated systems. Its executives should provide the records that establish what those systems were instructed to do, who authorised those instructions and why the No Kings account was suspended.  If Zuckerberg wants people to believe this was an innocent automated mistake, Meta should release the records that establish it. An apology isn’t evidence.  If you got this far, tell me what 2 + 2 equals. I doubt many will answer.

MEDIA RELEASE Imphal, the 19th October, 2026  TIM Condemns Khamenlok Killings of Three Meitei Civilians, Demands Prosecution of Jangboi Kipgen and End to Political Immunity  Thadou Inpi Manipur (TIM) strongly condemns the killing of three innocent Meitei civilians today near Khongban Sunurok (Khongbal), close to the Khamenlok area of Kangpokpi district, by suspected Kuki armed militant groups operating under the Suspension of Operations (SoO) agreement. Around 16 villagers collecting firewood were fired upon by assailants wearing red ribbons and carrying sophisticated firearms, who had positioned themselves behind a pile of cut firewood. The deceased are Lairenlakpam Inaobi (57), Arubam Ronin (35) and Kshetrimayum Susil (32); Inaobi and Ronin died at the spot while Susil succumbed en route to hospital. The injured — Ngangom Suraj (19), Meisnam Somendro (53) and Khomdram Bosan (45) — were taken to a private hospital in Imphal.  This is not an isolated incident. It forms part of a calculated pattern of violence engineered across successive flashpoints — Koutruk, Uyokching, Litan, the Imphal–Tamenglong (IT) Road, and now Khamenlok — under the unified command of Jangboi Kipgen, Home Secretary of KNF(P). He exercises unified command over all Kuki militants in Kangpokpi district, including SoO signatories under UPF and KNO such as KNA/KNO, KLA/KLO, KRA/KNO, KLA/KNO and other Kuki militant groups, including SoO and non-SoO groups like KNF-N.  The Khamenlok attack, coming immediately after the IT Road killings and the reported beheading of a Naga civilian, appears designed to divert attention from those atrocities while sustaining the cycle of bloodshed. Approximately 100 civilians have been killed in ethnic violence-related incidents since the beginning of 2026. Not a single perpetrator has been arrested or prosecuted, even in cases where armed militants filmed their crimes with faces uncovered and circulated the videos in social medias.  Political protection has enabled this impunity. The immunity extended to Jangboi Kipgen by Kuki Deputy Chief Minister Nemcha Kipgen and Kuki MLA Haokholet Kipgen must be exposed. They should not be welcomed or allowed free movement in Imphal while armed groups under their influence continue to operate with impunity in their constituencies and influenced area.  When Manipur has a Chief Minister who dances to the tune of armed militant groups, shows no leadership and does not care about the safety of ordinary citizens, and an administration that appears to be controlled by unelected, illegitimate armed groups, the elected government’s response is reduced to routinely issuing condemnations without taking effective action to bring perpetrators to justice or stop the killing spree. Are the Chief Minister and his Council of Ministers acting as proxies for certain armed militant mafia groups?  Kuki–Naga violence has escalated alarmingly, while Kuki–Meitei tensions have resumed after a period of relative calm, threatening further escalation and bloodshed. As perpetrators continue their appalling acts of violence, terror and killings without accountability, civilians continue to pay the price while politicians remain preoccupied with party politics and election campaigning.  If there is a responsible and functioning government in Manipur, it must act like one. Otherwise, it must resign rather than allow armed groups to reign terror on the state’s unarmed citizens. Killings and retaliatory killings have become a recurring, daily occurrence. TIM demands the immediate booking and prosecution of Jangboi Kipgen and all those responsible.  Issued by — Thadou Inpi Manipur  Statement: “Thadou is a distinct ethnic group of people. Thadou is not Kuki, or underneath Kuki, or part of Kuki, but a separate, independent entity from Kuki. Any organization that incorporates “Thadou” but espouses Kuki and mis-portrays Thadou as Kuki or a part of Kuki is illegitimate and does not represent Thadou people and interest” –

Imposing Sanctions to Protect Americans from Intellectual Property Theft 10/19/2026 10:44 AM EDT  Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman  Imposing Sanctions to Protect Americans from Intellectual Property Theft  Press Statement  October 19, 2026  Today, the Department of State is sanctioning five entities connected to People’s Republic of China national Linwei Ding under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (PAIPA) in connection with theft of trade secrets from U.S. persons. The United States has long been a leader in developing emerging technology. This theft of trade secrets is a serious threat to U.S. economic, foreign policy, and national security interests.  Today’s designations follow an investigation of Ding by the Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation. On January 29, 2026, a U.S. federal jury convicted Ding of seven counts of theft of trade secrets. Ding was convicted of stealing thousands of pages of confidential information containing Google’s trade secrets related to super intelligence (SI) technology to benefit himself and China-based tech companies.  Theft of trade secrets related to sensitive and emerging technologies harms U.S. jobs, companies, and investments, and costs U.S. industry billions of dollars each year. The Trump Administration remains committed to protecting American innovation and safeguarding Americans from intellectual property theft.    Today’s action is being taken pursuant to the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (50 U.S.C. 1709).  For more information on today’s action, please see the Department of State’s Fact Sheet.

AI agents are becoming the newest insiders in the enterprise. And that changes how we think about security.  As Satya Nadella highlights, we cannot rely on a model to police itself. The intelligence may sit inside the model, but the security controls must sit outside it.  Microsoft’s latest expansion of Project Perception puts this principle into practice with continuous risk assessment, adaptive permissions, and threat containment for AI agents.  Three principles stand out:  • Identity: Know which agent is acting, on whose behalf, and with what authority.  • Least privilege: Give agents only the access they need for a specific task, not unrestricted access to everything their human counterpart can access.  • Continuous oversight: Monitor behavior, reassess risk, and tighten permissions or stop an agent when something goes wrong.  The bigger shift is this: AI security cannot be a one-time approval. It must be a continuous process of observation, authorization, and containment.  As AI moves from generating answers to executing actions across enterprise systems, trust alone is not a security strategy. Architecture is.  The goal isn't to make AI incapable of making mistakes. It's to build systems where mistakes don't automatically become incidents.  That is what responsible agentic AI at enterprise scale should look like.  What do you think: are organizations building the security infrastructure for autonomous AI at the same pace they're deploying the agents themselves?  Read more: blogs.microsoft.com/blog/202…

🔴WAR ON TERRORISM: IRAN 🇮🇷🔴/Israel Hayom/  Another Iran round is inevitable, IDF chief of staff believes  Eight days before Israelis head to the polls, the IDF is on high alert for possible security developments, as some in the political leadership hint the military could strike Iran first for political reasons.  by Lilach Shoval   Eight days before the election, the IDF is on especially high alert for possible security developments.  As of now, senior officials say there is no concrete intelligence pointing to rising tensions.  Still, the defense establishment's biggest concern is that Iran might conclude Israel and the US will again try to catch Tehran off guard under cover of the election.  In such a scenario, the Iranians might try to seize the initiative this time, striking first in the belief that whoever moves first usually gains the upper hand.  The problem is that some in the political leadership may be trying to drop hints that Israel could strike first, for political reasons, heightening the risk of exactly that kind of Iranian miscalculation.  This is despite the fact that, according to senior defense officials, there is no urgent need to attack or take initiated action in the days leading up to the election.  Still, it's important to stress that top IDF brass emphasize the Iranian threat is far from over, and the chief of staff believes Israel will have to return to fighting at some stage.  When asked whether a return to fighting must happen before the election, senior officers say no.  Quite the opposite, in fact. Military leaders believe the top priority in the coming days, beyond preparing for surprises and unforeseen security developments, is ensuring stability and allowing the election to take place on schedule, as part of Israel's democratic process.  Reports claiming the Americans asked Israel to act alone, or that Israel is considering acting alone against Iran, should be treated with a great deal of skepticism, though Israel is also preparing for the possibility that it will be forced to go it alone if all other options run out.  It's worth noting that the relationship between the chief of staff, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, and his counterpart, the commander of CENTCOM, Admiral Brad Cooper, is strong, as are the ties between Israeli and American officers more broadly, which grew significantly closer during preparations for Operation Roaring Lion, during the operation itself, and afterward as well.  The working assumption is that if Israel returns to fighting, it will do so alongside the US. This is where the American calculation comes into play.  The last thing President Donald Trump needs or wants is to head into the midterm elections in the middle of an active war with Iran, with oil prices climbing.  But Iran isn't the only volatile front these days. As we saw this past weekend, Judea and Samaria are on the verge of erupting, with the army, police and Shin Bet failing, perhaps because they aren't trying hard enough, to rein in the chaos caused by hundreds of right-wing extremists who have been relentlessly attacking Palestinians during the olive harvest.  Along the way, they also managed over the weekend to harm an American press photographer and foreign diplomats from Poland, Belgium and France. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part, offered only a mild condemnation and a statement that the matter should be reviewed, language that hasn't done much to rein in events on the ground. To that, of course, must be added the constant tension in Lebanon and Gaza.  Either way, Chief of Staff Zamir and the entire IDF top brass have an important role to play in the coming days in maintaining security stability that will allow the election to proceed on schedule.  But there is no doubt the security challenges are far from over, and whatever government comes next will have to confront them, and sooner rather than later.  israelhayom.com/2026/10/18/i… via @israelhayom

The Houthis may be moving beyond assembling Iranian weapons and toward building more advanced ballistic missiles inside Yemen.  An arms-intelligence report cited by The National says the group is using imported precision components to develop missiles with greater range and maneuverability.  One reported Palestine-2 variant is estimated to reach about 1,800 kilometers, potentially making it harder for air defenses to intercept.  That matters because Houthi-controlled territory sits beside Bab el-Mandeb, a critical gateway between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.  Millions of barrels of oil and petroleum products pass through the chokepoint, while commercial ships already face threats from missiles and drones.  For the U.S., the concern goes beyond Yemen.  If the Houthis can threaten one of the world’s critical shipping routes, how long before the threat reaches American forces and the global economy?

sample_tweets.text: ⚠️ Threat Actor Offers 'Critical 0-Day' for Garuda Indonesia Financial API  A darkweb forum post alleges the discovery of a critical vulnerability in the financial infrastructure of Garuda Indonesia, a major Southeast Asian airline group. The threat actor claims to have identified an unauthenticated SOAP API endpoint that allows unauthorized access to the financial ledgers of multiple airline tenants within the group. The post, titled "Critical vulnerabilities for sale garuda-indonesia.com," lists the target as a "Major Southeast Asian Airline Group" and prices the exploit at $1,300.  According to the listing, the vulnerability is classified as a Broken Access Control or Missing Authentication issue with a claimed CVSS score of 10.0. The actor asserts that the server parameter in the API routes database operations without requiring any session, token, or multi-factor authentication. The post details several alleged capabilities enabled by this flaw:  *   **Redirect Money:** Changing the receiving bank account of approved payments to an attacker-controlled account. *   **Tamper Amounts:** Altering payment amounts, such as reducing a multi-billion IDR payment to 1 IDR. *   **Forge Approvals:** Erasing director approvals and forging verifier identities. *   **Dump Ledgers:** Downloading full financial data for over seven airline tenants without login credentials.  The thread includes a redacted Proof of Concept (PoC) demonstrating a baseline read and a subsequent update operation where the bank name was changed to "ATTACKER BANK 999" and the amount to "1.0000 IDR," with the system returning a success message. The actor claims the data was restored after the test. Exploitable endpoints listed include UpdatePayment, Verification, ResetApproval, GetReport, and SendToIssued.  Garuda Indonesia is the flag carrier of Indonesia and one of the largest airline groups in Southeast Asia, operating multiple brands including Citilink and TransNusa. A breach of this nature could expose sensitive financial records and potentially enable direct financial fraud if the claims are accurate. At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified by Garuda Indonesia or security researchers.

🚨 Threat Actor Claims Full Database Access to JAMCO Aerospace  A darkweb forum post alleges that a threat actor has obtained full database access to JAMCO Aerospace, a major aerospace and defense company. The post, published on October 17, 2026, by an actor using the handle 'OlliverQueen,' claims to possess comprehensive access to the company's internal data infrastructure.  JAMCO Aerospace is a prominent joint venture between the Saudi Arabian General Investment Authority (SAGIA) and the German aerospace group MTU Aero Engines AG. Headquartered in Riyadh, the company specializes in the manufacturing of aircraft engines and components for commercial and military aviation. As a critical player in the global supply chain for aircraft propulsion systems, the organization holds significant intellectual property regarding engine design, manufacturing processes, and proprietary technical specifications.  The threat actor's track record suggests a pattern of targeting large multinational corporations and financial institutions with claims of database breaches. Recent posts by 'OlliverQueen' on underground forums include alleged leaks of customer data from GXS Bank in Singapore, LTIMindtree (LTM), Optum, and AOL, often accompanied by samples of sensitive personal information such as names, addresses, phone numbers, and account details. The actor typically monetizes these claims by selling access or specific datasets for cryptocurrency payments.  If authentic, the exposure of JAMCO Aerospace's database could have severe implications for the defense sector, potentially enabling industrial espionage, theft of trade secrets, or targeted attacks on supply chain partners. However, no independent verification of this specific claim has been provided, and JAMCO Aerospace has not yet publicly commented on the allegation. At the time of reporting, the alleged breach remains unverified.  #JAMCOAerospace #DataBreach #AerospaceSecurity #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity

🚨 Threat Actor Claims Full Breach of Liga MX Internal Database  A post on an underground forum alleges that the central internal database of Liga MX and the Mexican Football Federation (FMF), known as SIID, has been fully extracted. The threat actor claims to have obtained sensitive operational data, including production database connection strings, JWT signing keys, and password encryption passphrases, which could potentially allow for further unauthorized access to the platform's infrastructure.  According to the listing, the stolen data includes a significant volume of user and player records:  - 12,679 user accounts (out of 13,171 registered) with passwords stored in plain text across LIGA MX, FMF, club, MLS, and federation portals - 334 salary records for Liga MX and Expansión BBVA players, detailing contract IDs, monthly amounts in MXN, and payment counts - 336 player files containing CURP (Mexican national ID), RFC (tax ID), and medical data such as blood type, Rh factor, allergies, height, and weight - 799 official Fan ID tickets in PDF format - 4,193 internal SQL query files from the entire platform - 5 production database connection strings (LIGAMX\PRIMARYDB, FMF\DBFMF, Amateur\SAF) along with SMTP credentials  Liga MX is the top professional football league in Mexico, operating under the umbrella of the Mexican Football Federation. The exposure of plain-text credentials and production database keys represents a severe security failure if authentic, as it could enable lateral movement within the organization's network. The inclusion of medical and financial data for players raises significant privacy concerns under Mexican data protection laws.  The identity of the threat actor remains unknown, as the post was made by an unverified user on the forum. At the time of reporting, neither Liga MX nor the FMF has publicly acknowledged the breach, and the claims regarding the data extraction have not been independently verified.  #DataBreach #LigaMX #FootballSecurity #DarkWeb #CyberSecurity #Mexico

🚨 Threat Actor Claims Breach of Cambridge University Press Digital Platform  A post on an underground forum alleges that a threat actor has compromised the digital learning platform of Cambridge University Press & Assessment, specifically targeting the 'Cambridge One' service. The actor claims to have extracted significant amounts of data from the platform's infrastructure, which reportedly runs on ComproDLS, SAP Gigya, AWS, and Okta.  According to the listing, the alleged breach exposes a wide range of sensitive assets, including: - 100,999 objects from the content database - 11 tenant organization IDs, including Cambridge, Elsevier, VHL, and Swinburne - 6 production identity site API keys - 3 Cognito identity groups with verified accounts and live tokens - 113 mapped subdomains across production, development, QA, hotfix, release, and alpha environments - Internal corporate RBAC documentation - Corporate GitHub credentials embedded in the database - Access to the platform's AWS account with renewable credentials - Reusable token/session exchange recipes for various environments  Cambridge University Press & Assessment is a major global publisher and assessment provider, serving educational institutions worldwide. The platform allegedly affected hosts content for multiple high-profile organizations, suggesting that if the claims are authentic, the breach could impact not only Cambridge's own data but also that of its partners. The exposure of API keys, AWS credentials, and internal documentation could potentially enable further lateral movement or intellectual property theft.  The threat actor has attached three files to the post: proof_sample.txt, org_matrix.txt, and bucket_listing_extract.txt. At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified by Cambridge University Press or security researchers.

🚨 Threat Actor Claims Breach of Serbian Insurer Triglav, Exposing 525k Records  A threat actor has claimed to have breached Triglav, one of Serbia's largest insurance companies, and extracted a customer database containing over 525,000 records. According to the post on an underground forum, the stolen data spans from 2020 to 2026 and includes highly sensitive personal information for policyholders.  The actor alleges that the compromised dataset contains the following fields: - Full names and dates of birth - JMBG (Unique Master Citizen Number), which is equivalent to a Social Security Number or national ID - Travel document numbers - Detailed residential addresses, including city, postal code, street, entrance number, and apartment number - Insurance start and expiration dates  The post includes a sample of the data, showing specific entries with names, JMBGs, and addresses in cities such as Novi Sad, Belgrade, and Stara Pazova. The actor issued a notice to Triglav, offering to negotiate for the permanent deletion of the data. If no agreement is reached, the threat actor claims the full database will be published on October 18, 2026.  Triglav is a major player in the Serbian insurance market, providing life, health, and property insurance services to a significant portion of the population. The exposure of JMBGs and detailed address information poses a severe risk of identity theft and targeted fraud for affected individuals.

sample_tweets.text: 💳🔐 YOUR CREDIT CARD NUMBER ISN’T RANDOM — HERE’S HOW IT ACTUALLY WORKS  Ever wondered why credit cards have 15 or 16 digits? Or how payment systems can detect an incorrectly entered card number almost instantly?  There’s mathematics behind it.  Most payment card numbers follow an international numbering standard (ISO/IEC 7812) and use a checksum algorithm called Luhn.  Here’s what’s hiding inside those digits:  🔎 1. The First 6–8 Digits: IIN/BIN  These identify the card issuer and help payment networks route transactions.  Visa commonly starts with 4 Mastercard uses ranges including 51–55 and 2221–2720 American Express uses 34 or 37  🔢 2. The Middle Digits: Account Identifier  These form part of the issuer-assigned account number. Their length varies depending on the card’s numbering structure.  🧮 3. The Final Digit: Luhn Checksum  The final digit is calculated using the Luhn algorithm, a mathematical technique designed to detect common typing errors.  But here’s the interesting part:  A card number passing the Luhn check does NOT mean the card actually exists.  It also doesn’t prove the account is active, has available funds, or is authorized for transactions.  ⚠️ DDW Analyst Note:  Attackers can generate numbers that satisfy mathematical checksum rules. That’s why payment security cannot depend on card-number validation alone.  Modern payment protection relies on multiple layers, including issuer authorization, fraud detection, tokenization, and transaction authentication.  Understanding how card numbers work is useful. Understanding what they cannot prove is even more important.  📊 See our infographic for a visual breakdown.  #DailyDarkWeb #CyberSecurity #PaymentSecurity #FraudPrevention

🇦🇷 🚨 ARGENTINA: THREAT ACTORS CLAIM 1 MILLION-RECORD DATABASE FROM TUCUMÁN PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT  A threat actor group on an underground forum has posted what it describes as a database from the provincial government of Tucumán, Argentina.  The listing claims: * About 1 million records, 1.5 GB in total * Full names * Municipality and province * Home addresses, with more fields listed  The post credits several group members and a collaborating actor. Its proof images did not load, so no sample was visible.  The claim has not been independently verified.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: If genuine, a province-wide list of names and home addresses is useful for phishing and fraud that pretends to come from provincial services. The same group posted a similar listing for Mexico's Yucatán state government on the same day, which points to a run of attacks on Latin American regional government sites. Unverified threat-actor claim, NOT confirmation of a compromise of Tucumán government systems.  Source: this is for subscribers only. 🇦🇹 🚨 LOXONE CONFIRMS CYBERATTACK ON INTERNAL SYSTEMS; SAYS BUILDING CONTROLS UNAFFECTED  Austrian building-automation vendor LOXONE says it detected a cyberattack on internal company systems on Sunday, Oct 18, 2026. In an Oct 19 press release and website notice, it says the affected systems were isolated immediately, external IT forensics specialists are involved, and the relevant authorities have been informed.  What LOXONE says (Oct 19 update, 13:01 CEST): • Miniserver, Remote Connect and Exosphere are not affected; Miniservers run locally and do not need LOXONE servers or the internet to work • User and access credentials are stored locally on the Miniserver, not at LOXONE • Affected internal systems include CRM systems with data on partner companies, plus applicant data; it is still checking exactly which data is affected and will notify those affected directly • It has identified the attack vector but is not disclosing it, and is bringing systems back step by step  ⚠️ Analyst Note: That customer installations are unaffected is LOXONE's own assessment. LOXONE has not said what data, if any, was taken, who was behind the attack, or how many people are affected. Partners and job applicants should treat incident-themed emails with caution and contact LOXONE only through its official channels.  Source: loxone.com/enen/  Press release (PDF): loxone.com/assets/files/2026… #DDW #LOXONE #Cybersecurity #CyberAttack #BuildingAutomation #ThreatIntelligence

🇯🇵 🚨 UPDATE: JAPAN ALERT-MAIL SUPPLIER ARCADIA SAYS ITS HACKED SYSTEMS SENT 1,423,428 UNAUTHORIZED EMAILS  Osaka-based Arcadia Inc., which runs the SpeeCAN RAIDEN disaster-alert mail service used by Japanese municipalities, published a detailed report on Oct 19, 2026 about the breach it first disclosed on Oct 13.  What's new in Arcadia's report: • A malicious program sent 1,423,428 emails to outside recipients. Many looked like balance-check messages from credit card companies and are suspected phishing • Entry point: a directory path-traversal flaw on a media server that hosts attachments exposed internal source files, including a config file holding a service-to-service login secret key • The attackers used that key to brute-force account IDs, then pulled internal data from the logged-in sessions • Arcadia found a backdoor on Oct 13 (Japan time) after noticing the mass mailing, and stopped the unauthorized sending that morning • All services were fully restored on Oct 15. A third-party security firm will run a deeper investigation, and Arcadia plans to file a damage report with police • For NET119 (text-based 119 emergency reporting), possible exposure is now put at personal data linked to 9,020 email addresses, down from the earlier estimate of up to ~13,000 users  Municipal impact: Shizuoka City says registrant data for its disaster-alert mail leaked (email addresses of 34,336 residents, plus names, staff numbers and departments of 6,915 city employees). It also documented fake "credit card company" emails sent from the genuine alert-mail sender domain.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: The 1,423,428 figure counts emails sent, not unique recipients or confirmed phishing victims. The total and the attack chain are vendor-reported, and the investigation continues. No ransomware group or leak claim has been attributed, and this is not a new attack. Because the messages came from real alert-mail infrastructure, they may have passed normal sender checks. Recipients should treat card "usage confirmation" emails from alert-mail addresses as fraud.  Source: raiden.site.ktaiwork.jp/arch… city.shizuoka.lg.jp/s4268/s0… #DDW #Arcadia #DataBreach #Japan #Phishing #PublicSafety

🇺🇸 🚨 BULLHORN CYBER INCIDENT TAKES STAFFING PLATFORM OFFLINE; USERS MUST RESET PASSWORDS  Recruitment and staffing software provider Bullhorn confirmed on Oct 17, 2026 that it detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. It temporarily disabled access to its systems to contain the activity and says it is working with cybersecurity specialists from CrowdStrike.  Bullhorn's Oct 19 status update (5:00 AM ET): • AUS and EMEA/UK systems are back online; US availability was estimated for 4–7 AM ET on Oct 19 • All non-SSO users must reset their password when they log in • Bullhorn is investigating login issues for SSO customers, and some users may hit a loop while updating passwords  For API users and integrations, per Bullhorn's customer FAQ: • API-user passwords have been expired; integrations hosted by customers or third parties need the new password in their code/config • Bullhorn-hosted integrations are handled by Bullhorn, and Marketplace partners will be contacted directly • Client Secret rotation will be required later, but not yet  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Bullhorn says its forensic investigation is ongoing and it has not yet determined whether customer data was exfiltrated. It has not disclosed the entry method, a threat actor, or how many customers are affected, and restoration times may still change. Staffing firms should only reset passwords through Bullhorn's own login flow and treat unexpected "reset your Bullhorn password" emails with caution.  Source: status.bullhorn.com/incident…  Customer FAQ: docs.google.com/document/d/e… #DDW #Bullhorn #CyberIncident #SaaS #Staffing #ThreatIntelligence

🇲🇽 🚨 MEXICO: HACKERS CLAIM FULL DATA LEAK FROM GUERRERO STATE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION  A threat actor group on an underground forum has posted what it calls a full leak from the Guerrero State Ministry of Education (SEG), the agency that runs public and private schooling in the Mexican state of Guerrero.  The actor claims about 28,000 records plus government mail, including: * Employee INE voter ID cards and SEG staff ID cards * CURP, NSS (social security) and RFC (tax ID) numbers * Bank accounts, salaries, payroll codes and pay stubs * Personnel files, certificates and appointments * Official email addresses with their passwords and login details  The actor says the files are being given away for free through its own channel.  The claim has not been independently verified.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: If genuine, this is a serious exposure for teachers and education staff: ID documents plus bank and payroll data are enough for identity theft and payroll-diversion fraud. Working government email logins would also let attackers send phishing from real SEG addresses. Password resets on SEG mail and checks on payroll changes are the urgent steps. Unverified threat-actor claim, NOT confirmation of a compromise of SEG systems.  Source: this is for subscribers only. 🇷🇺 🚨 FIRSTVDS CONFIRMS ATTACKERS STOLE CUSTOMER SERVER DATA THROUGH A VMMANAGER 6 FLAW  Russian hosting provider FirstVDS says attackers got into part of its infrastructure on Oct 17, 2026 through a vulnerability in VMmanager 6, its virtualization management system.  According to the provider: • A data-stealing program ran on some virtualization nodes, mounted customer VM disks read-only, and sent the copied data to the attackers' server • Copied data included passwords, SSH/API/cloud access keys and tokens, config files and command history, crypto wallets, and user files • The program changed nothing on the disks and never ran inside the VMs, so affected servers show no traces and keep running normally • Only part of the infrastructure was hit; affected customers were notified in their account panel and by email, with more notices sent Oct 18  Oct 19 update (7:20 AM MSK): the VMmanager vendor released another fix overnight and FirstVDS has installed it, but the flaw is not fully closed. External access to the management system stays shut until further patches ship.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Notified customers should treat everything stored on the server as copied. FirstVDS advises moving crypto funds to new wallets made on a clean device, changing and revoking (not just replacing) all passwords, SSH keys, API keys and tokens, and checking logins after Oct 17, plus authorized_keys, new users, cron jobs and systemd services. FirstVDS has not said how many customers were affected, and no CVE ID or affected VMmanager build range has been published. Other VMmanager 6 operators should watch for vendor patches and keep the panel off the internet.  Source: t.me/s/TakeFirstNews/1463 #DDW #FirstVDS #VMmanager #DataBreach #Hosting #ThreatIntelligence

🇸🇨 🚨 AL SALAM BANK SEYCHELLES: 18 MILLION RECORDS ALLEGEDLY LEAKED  A threat actor on an underground forum claims to be offering a database of 18 million records allegedly taken from Al Salam Bank Seychelles.  The actor claims the dataset includes: * Customer transaction logs * Partial payment card numbers * One-time passwords (OTPs) * Internal bank identifiers  Samples shared by the actor appear to show activity from July 2026.  The claim has not been independently verified.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: If authentic, transaction history combined with OTP traffic points to a compromise of the bank's card-processing or SMS notification systems rather than a simple customer list. That gives fraudsters what they need for convincing bank-impersonation calls and account takeover. A similar claim about the bank's SMS transaction alerts surfaced in late September, so this may be the same data repackaged. Customers should watch their accounts and never share OTPs.  We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim, NOT confirmation of a breach of Al Salam Bank Seychelles systems.  Source: this is for subscribers only. 🇺🇸 🚨 COINTRACKER: 2.7 MILLION USER RECORDS ALLEGEDLY FOR SALE  A threat actor on an underground forum claims to be selling a database of more than 2.7 million user records allegedly linked to CoinTracker, the crypto portfolio and tax platform.  The actor claims the dataset includes: * Full names * Dates of birth and gender * Home addresses, city and ZIP code * Email addresses * Phone numbers * Account status  The claim has not been independently verified.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: If authentic, names, addresses and phone numbers tied to crypto holders are a strong target list for phishing, SIM-swap attempts and even physical threats. The newest records in the sample date to early 2025, and the field set looks more like a generic profile export than a typical crypto-tax account, so the data may be older or mislabeled. Users should be wary of any message referencing their account.  We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim, NOT confirmation of a breach of CoinTracker systems. 🇦🇪 🚨 UAE: THREAT ACTOR CLAIMS LEAK OF UAE FOOTBALL ASSOCIATION DATABASES AND 70K+ DOCUMENTS  A threat actor on an underground forum claims to have leaked the databases and documents of the UAE Football Association (UAE FA), the national governing body for football in the United Arab Emirates, and is offering them for sale.  The actor claims: * 130 million total records, of which about 15 million are described as important and the rest as logs and voting data * About 8 GB of databases across 500+ tables * More than 70,000 documents (around 100 GB; the listing title says 122 GB)  The listing includes what appears to be a scanned UAE identity card as a sample (fully redacted here).  The claim has not been independently verified.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: If genuine, identity documents of players, staff or officials would be the most sensitive part, since they enable identity fraud and targeted scams. Internal documents and voting records could also be politically sensitive inside the sport. The seller account is brand new. Unverified threat-actor claim, NOT confirmation of a compromise of UAE FA systems.  Source: this is for subscribers only. 🇳🇱 🚨 NETHERLANDS: THREAT ACTOR CLAIMS TO SELL PICNIC ONLINE SUPERMARKET DATABASE AND SOURCE CODE  A threat actor on an underground forum has posted a sale listing for data allegedly taken from Picnic, the online supermarket and grocery delivery service operating in the Netherlands.  According to the listing, the offer includes: * Picnic's full database * Picnic's full source code  No record count, sample or price was visible in the listing.
